paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP) is a parkinsonism that responds to levodopa. Pathologically it shows highly selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the zona compacta of the substantia nigra (Matsumine et al., 1997). In Japanese families, onset was early, with a mean age at onset of 27.8 years, progression was slow, and parkinsonian symptoms improved after sleep. Foot dystonia and hyperreflexia were common, and levodopa-induced dyskinesias and wearing-off occurred frequently (Ishikawa and Tsuji, 1996). Kitada et al. (1998) showed that the disorder is caused by mutations in the gene encoding parkin, and mutations in this gene were later found in patients whose phenotype resembled typical idiopathic Parkinson disease (Klein et al., 2000; Poorkaj et al., 2004).

paragraphs.text: Takahashi et al. (1994) described a family in which the parents were first cousins and 4 of 5 sibs developed parkinsonism at an early age. The parkinsonism improved after sleep. One sib, a 67-year-old woman, came to autopsy. Pathologic changes were confined to the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNPC) and the locus ceruleus. The medial and ventrolateral regions of the SNPC showed obvious neuronal loss and gliosis. In the rest of the SNPC and in the locus ceruleus, neurons were reduced in number and most had low melanin content, but there was no detectable gliosis or extraneuronal free melanin pigment. There were no Lewy bodies, and the authors considered the overall pathologic picture different from that of Lewy body Parkinson disease.

paragraphs.text: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) described 17 patients from 12 Japanese families with familial juvenile parkinsonism suggesting autosomal recessive inheritance. Affected individuals were predominantly female, the mean age at onset was 27.8 years, and progression was slow. The parkinsonian triad of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia was mild. Gait freezing, hyperreflexia, foot dystonia, and retropulsion were relatively prominent. In all patients, parkinsonian symptoms improved after sleep. The response to levodopa was satisfactory, but dopa-induced choreic limb dyskinesia and the wearing-off phenomenon were frequent. The authors concluded that AR-JP is a distinct clinical entity.

paragraphs.text: Chien et al. (2006) studied a genetic isolate from northeastern Brazil with early-onset Parkinson disease (average age at onset 30.8 years) and multiple consanguineous marriages.
